justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across all three horizons, starting near current market levels and gradually trending higher. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 135.8 is essentially anchored to recent price action, with only minimal expected movement given typical daily volatility patterns. For the one-week estimate of 136.5, I incorporated a slight positive drift assumption based on the prevailing trend, while acknowledging that mean-reversion pressures and short-term noise could easily offset any directional bias. The one-month estimate of 137.5 extends that same gentle upward trajectory, reflecting a baseline assumption of modest appreciation without any strong fundamental catalyst pushing prices sharply in either direction.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical volatility at each time horizon. Daily intervals are naturally tighter because there are fewer opportunities for large shocks to accumulate, while weekly and monthly intervals widen substantially to reflect the compounding of uncertainty over time. The one-month interval spanning roughly 122 to 153 is deliberately wide because a full calendar month exposes the forecast to multiple rounds of macroeconomic data, earnings releases, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments — any of which could shift sentiment materially. I also weighted recent realized volatility somewhat higher than long-run averages, which contributed to the relatively wide monthly band.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include sudden shifts in monetary policy expectations, particularly if central bank guidance surprises markets in either a hawkish or dovish direction. On the downside, a deterioration in risk sentiment driven by geopolitical escalation, a credit event, or a sharper-than-expected economic slowdown could push prices well below the lower bound of the monthly interval. On the upside, a strongly positive surprise in economic data or a resolution of existing geopolitical tensions combined with renewed liquidity injections could push prices above the upper bound.

It is also worth noting that tail risks are inherently underrepresented in symmetric confidence intervals. Fat-tailed distributions — which financial assets tend to exhibit in practice — mean that extreme moves are more probable than a normal distribution would imply. A flash crash, a sudden liquidity shock, or an unexpected policy announcement could all produce moves that fall outside even the wide monthly interval I provided. Readers should treat these estimates as probabilistic guides rather than firm predictions, and they should be especially cautious about treating the interval bounds as hard floors or ceilings.
